Title: Returning to the Traditional Foundation of Marriage: Why Same-Sex Marriage Rights should be repealed

Introduction

The institution of marriage is an integral cornerstone of our society, providing a stable platform from which families grow and human relationships flourish. Over time, the definition of marriage has evolved, expanding to include new ideas and pushing the envelope of what is considered the "traditional" model. The issue at hand is whether same-sex marriage rights belong within the legal definition of marriage or if, indeed, the rights should be repealed and returned to the earlier definition of being "between one man and one woman." I argue that repealing same-sex marriage rights and restoring the legal definition of marriage as between one man and one woman is crucial to uphold the sanctity of marriage and the moral values that have historically kept society intact.

I. Marriage as a Basis of Society

Marriage has been an essential unit of society, bringing together two individuals seeking to provide mutual support, companionship, and stability within a committed union. The traditional model of a heterosexual marriage is rooted not only in historical context but also biological and religious law. From a biological perspective, the union of a man and a woman serves to ensure the continuation of the human species as it makes reproduction possible.

Moreover, marriage as a religious institution is founded on the belief that it is ordained by God. The Biblical definition of marriage designates it a sacred union between a man and a woman, which further shapes societal beliefs. As such, to alter the meaning of this sacred institution may offend those whose faith underpins their values, morals, and way of life. By rejecting the same-sex marriage rights recognized by the Obergefell v. Hodges decision in 2015, we can uphold religious freedom and prevent the infringement upon the beliefs of those who adhere to the traditional definition of marriage.

II. The Slippery Slope

Expanding the legal definition of marriage may lead society down a slippery slope where alternative lifestyles become increasingly accepted. Admittedly, this might seem far-fetched, but consider the striking difference between the current definition of marriage and what society traditionally acknowledged. Would it be a stretch to see other alternative unions, such as polygamous relationships, seeking legal recognition as well?

The legal definition of marriage should have clear and firm boundaries such as one man and one woman. We need to consider the potential consequences of what may happen if we open the door of legal unions to any subjective interpretation of love and commitment. By maintaining stronger boundaries on the parameters of marriage, we can prevent potential chaos in the judicial system, as well as the turmoil within social norms and family structures.

III. Protecting the Sanctity of Marriage

The inclusion of same-sex marriage within the legal definition of marriage overall dilutes the sanctity of marriage as an institution. Marriage has long been associated with commitment and loyalty, and the dissolution of the relationship is not taken lightly in either religious or cultural contexts. Divorce rates in the United States have soared over recent decades, revealing the increasing fragility of the legal union.

By narrowing the definition of marriage to one man and one woman, we strengthen not only the institution of marriage but also the value of the union itself. We must ensure that all partnerships are built on a foundation of deep commitment and loyalty, thus restoring the reputation of marriage in society.

Conclusion

The issue of same-sex marriage rights has long been a contentious one, provoking intense reactions on both sides. However, it is crucial to remember the historical, religious, and biological foundations upon which the institution of marriage was built. By repealing same-sex marriage rights and restoring a legal definition of "one man, one woman," we can protect the sanctity of the institution, prevent society from venturing down a slippery slope, and uphold the moral values that keep our society intact. In turn, the traditional definition of marriage will once again be recognized as a critical cornerstone of our society, providing the stability and nurturing environment necessary for the human family to flourish.

  • Moral consistency with sexual ethics: Advocates argue opposite-sex exclusivity enforces norms that channel sexual desire productively, link sex to responsibility (potential offspring), and avoid normalizing relationships detached from reproduction. Proponents cite higher rates of emotional stability, educational attainment, and lower involvement in crime or poverty when raised by biological mother-father dyads. Redefining marriage (per this view) shifts emphasis from child interests to adult fulfillment, potentially increasing family instability.
  • Societal reproduction and sustainability: Societies must replace themselves; opposite-sex marriage is framed as the sole mechanism for natural population continuity without reliance on technology or migration. Countries with low fertility and high same-sex marriage adoption are sometimes pointed to as illustrative of broader trends in delayed childbearing and family fragmentation.
  • Reduced externalities on public policy: Traditional marriage correlates in some datasets with lower welfare dependency, better intergenerational wealth transfer, and community cohesion. Broadening access is argued to increase costs via expanded benefits (inheritance, tax credits, adoption rights) without the offsetting reproductive benefit.
  • Deterrence of alternative family forms: Exclusive recognition is said to discourage cohabitation, single parenthood, and blended non-biological arrangements by maintaining a clear "gold standard" tied to biological reality.

Cultural and Symbolic Arguments

  • Preservation of historical and anthropological pattern: Marriage as man-woman exists across virtually all recorded societies and civilizations, often tied to rites of passage, inheritance rules, and alliances. Organizations like the Heritage Foundation, Family Research Council, or scholars such as Mark Regnerus (controversial same-sex parenting study) or David Blankenhorn articulate population-level rationales.
